analysis.one_liner: Repeals every part of the Affordable Care Act the Supreme Court did not strike down.
analysis.headline: A one-sponsor bill to repeal the Affordable Care Act, introduced the same day the Supreme Court upheld it, died in committee with zero cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the Affordable Care Act and the health provisions of the 2010 reconciliation law — with a twist. It repealed only the parts the Supreme Court had 'not declared unconstitutional' in its June 28, 2012 decision. Since the Court struck down nothing that day (it upheld the law's individual mandate as a tax), the bill as written would have repealed the entire health reform law: coverage subsidies, the Medicaid expansion, protections for people with preexisting conditions, and the 3.8% tax on investment income for high earners.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the largest winners would be high-income households, who would stop paying the Affordable Care Act's 3.8% Medicare tax on investment income, and people who would otherwise owe the individual-mandate penalty. Health insurers and drug makers would be freed from the law's rules, but insurers would also lose the millions of subsidized customers the law steers to them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners and households facing the mandate penalty

how_it_helps.text: Repealing the health title of the 2010 reconciliation law would eliminate the Affordable Care Act's 3.8% Medicare tax on investment income, which applies mainly to households with income above $200,000 for individuals and $250,000 for couples.
Repealing the law would end the individual mandate, so people who chose not to buy insurance would no longer owe a penalty.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the cost. Millions of people would lose subsidized coverage and the Medicaid expansion would disappear; people with preexisting conditions would again face denial or priced-out insurance; young adults would lose the right to stay on a parent's plan; seniors would lose the closing of the Medicare drug 'donut hole' and pay more out of pocket.
analysis.who_pays_short: The uninsured, people with preexisting conditions, seniors

drawbacks.text: Repeal would strip coverage protections from people who gained them under the law, including bans on denying coverage for preexisting conditions and subsidies that help low- and middle-income families buy insurance.

The bill's own formula made it a full repeal: because the Supreme Court's June 28, 2012 decision struck down no part of the law — it upheld the individual mandate as a constitutional exercise of Congress's taxing power — everything would fall under the bill's instruction to repeal what was 'not declared unconstitutional.'
Repeal would raise costs for hospitals and state budgets, since the law's coverage expansion was paired with payment cuts to hospitals to offset the cost of care for the uninsured.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tax relief for high earners and the end of the mandate penalty are real but narrow, while the losses — subsidized coverage, preexisting-condition protections, the Medicaid expansion, and seniors' drug discounts — fall broadly on people who gained under the law. As a piece of policy, it would trade broad coverage gains for a repeal whose largest direct financial winners are at the top of the income scale.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced the same day the Supreme Court upheld the health care law, referred to eight House committees, never got a hearing or a vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Connie Mack introduced the bill on June 28, 2012 — the same day the Supreme Court upheld the Affordable Care Act's individual mandate in its ruling.
The bill was referred to eight House committees, including Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Judiciary, and later to several of their subcommittees.
No committee ever acted on it and no cosponsor signed on; the bill died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained anything from the bill itself; the practical effect is that the Affordable Care Act's coverage expansions, protections, and taxes stayed in place because the repeal never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the repeal simply died

for.name: Rep. Connie Mack
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the day of the Supreme Court's ruling and referred it to eight committees; no one else signed on.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican sponsor introduced it with zero cosponsors from either party, and it died without any vote that would show a partisan split.

industries.note: Repealing the 2010 reconciliation law's health title would end the 3.8% Medicare tax on investment income, borne mainly by households over the $200,000/$250,000 income thresholds. That gain comes directly from repeal, while the coverage losses fall on people far below those thresholds.

Repeal would free insurers from the law's rating rules and benefit mandates, but would also strip away the individual mandate and subsidies that steer millions of paying customers to them. Their net interest is genuinely two-sided here.

The law closed the Medicare 'donut hole,' discounting brand-name drugs for seniors; repeal would end those discounts, restoring higher out-of-pocket drug costs for older Americans while restoring drug makers' revenue on Medicare sales.

Hospitals accepted Medicare and Medicaid payment cuts under the law in exchange for the coverage expansion that reduced unpaid bills; repeal would take away the coverage while keeping nothing, leaving hospitals to absorb more uncompensated care.
